claim: Microglia continuously monitor synapses in mature healthy brains.
source: Microglia continuously monitor synapses, but active synaptic remodeling by microglia in mature healthy brains is rarely directly observed.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established context for the study.

claim: Active synaptic remodeling by microglia in mature healthy brains is rarely directly observed.
source: Microglia continuously monitor synapses, but active synaptic remodeling by microglia in mature healthy brains is rarely directly observed.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established context for the study.

claim: Photodamage focally increased the duration of microglia-neuron contacts.
source: The photodamage focally increased the duration of microglia-neuron contacts, and dramatically exacerbated both the turnover of dendritic spines and presynaptic boutons as well as the generation of new filopodia originating from spine heads or boutons.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Photodamage dramatically exacerbated the turnover of dendritic spines.
source: The photodamage focally increased the duration of microglia-neuron contacts, and dramatically exacerbated both the turnover of dendritic spines and presynaptic boutons as well as the generation of new filopodia originating from spine heads or boutons.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Photodamage dramatically exacerbated the turnover of presynaptic boutons.
source: The photodamage focally increased the duration of microglia-neuron contacts, and dramatically exacerbated both the turnover of dendritic spines and presynaptic boutons as well as the generation of new filopodia originating from spine heads or boutons.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Photodamage increased the generation of new filopodia originating from spine heads or boutons.
source: The photodamage focally increased the duration of microglia-neuron contacts, and dramatically exacerbated both the turnover of dendritic spines and presynaptic boutons as well as the generation of new filopodia originating from spine heads or boutons.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Elevated spine turnover is a microglia-dependent process.
source: The results of microglia depletion confirmed that elevated spine turnover and the generation of presynaptic filopodia are microglia-dependent processes.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by microglia depletion experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: The generation of presynaptic filopodia is a microglia-dependent process.
source: The results of microglia depletion confirmed that elevated spine turnover and the generation of presynaptic filopodia are microglia-dependent processes.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by microglia depletion experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Microglia are highly motile cells that regularly survey their environment within the central nervous system.
source: Microglia are highly motile cells that regularly survey their environment within the central nervous system and are responsible for immune defence in the brain (Nimmerjahn et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Nimmerjahn et al., 2005.

claim: Microglia are responsible for immune defence in the brain.
source: Microglia are highly motile cells that regularly survey their environment within the central nervous system and are responsible for immune defence in the brain (Nimmerjahn et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Nimmerjahn et al., 2005.

claim: Activation of microglia in response to infection or during ischemia, stroke and CNS trauma results in a release of different inflammatory signaling mediators.
source: Activation of microglia in response to infection or during ischemia, stroke and CNS trauma results in a release of different inflammatory signaling mediators (Davies et al., 2019; Greenhalgh et al., 2020) and can be associated with synaptic elimination by microglia (Brown and Neher, 2014; Wake et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Davies et al., 2019 and Greenhalgh et al., 2020.

claim: Activation of microglia can be associated with synaptic elimination by microglia.
source: Activation of microglia in response to infection or during ischemia, stroke and CNS trauma results in a release of different inflammatory signaling mediators (Davies et al., 2019; Greenhalgh et al., 2020) and can be associated with synaptic elimination by microglia (Brown and Neher, 2014; Wake et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Brown and Neher, 2014 and Wake et al., 2009.

claim: Non-activated microglia in the healthy mouse brain can interact with synapses.
source: Also, non-activated microglia in the healthy mouse brain can interact with synapses (Davalos et al., 2005; Wake et al., 2009) and thus play a critical role in neural circuit remodeling and brain plasticity during the development of the brain (Akiyoshi et al., 2018; Miyamoto et al., 2016; Paolicelli et al., 2011; Weinhard et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Davalos et al., 2005 and Wake et al., 2009.

claim: Non-activated microglia play a critical role in neural circuit remodeling and brain plasticity during the development of the brain.
source: Also, non-activated microglia in the healthy mouse brain can interact with synapses (Davalos et al., 2005; Wake et al., 2009) and thus play a critical role in neural circuit remodeling and brain plasticity during the development of the brain (Akiyoshi et al., 2018; Miyamoto et al., 2016; Paolicelli et al., 2011; Weinhard et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Akiyoshi et al., 2018; Miyamoto et al., 2016; Paolicelli et al., 2011; Weinhard et al., 2018.

claim: Microglia employ complement-dependent mechanisms to eliminate synapses during brain development.
source: At this stage, microglia employ complement-dependent mechanisms to eliminate synapses (Schafer et al., 2012; Stevens et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Schafer et al., 2012 and Stevens et al., 2007.

claim: In mature brains, microglia constantly make brief direct contacts with pre- and postsynaptic elements.
source: In mature brains, microglia constantly make brief direct contacts with pre- and postsynaptic elements (Akiyoshi et al., 2018; Nimmerjahn et al., 2005; Reshef et al., 2017; Wake et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Akiyoshi et al., 2018; Nimmerjahn et al., 2005; Reshef et al., 2017; Wake et al., 2009.

claim: The frequency of microglia contacts with synapses is increased during synaptic plasticity at postnatal day P30.
source: The frequency of contacts is increased during synaptic plasticity at postnatal day P30 (Pfeiffer et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Pfeiffer et al., 2016.

claim: The interaction between microglia and neurons contributes to synaptic modulation during motor learning (P30 and P60).
source: The interaction between microglia and neurons has been demonstrated to contribute to synaptic modulation during motor learning (P30 and P60) (Parkhurst et al., 2013), sensory plasticity (P30) (Tremblay et al., 2010), forgetting of remote memories (P70–P84) (Wang et al., 2020), and chronic stress-related synaptic remodeling (P60-120) (Milior et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Parkhurst et al., 2013.

claim: The interaction between microglia and neurons contributes to sensory plasticity (P30).
source: The interaction between microglia and neurons has been demonstrated to contribute to synaptic modulation during motor learning (P30 and P60) (Parkhurst et al., 2013), sensory plasticity (P30) (Tremblay et al., 2010), forgetting of remote memories (P70–P84) (Wang et al., 2020), and chronic stress-related synaptic remodeling (P60-120) (Milior et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tremblay et al., 2010.

claim: The interaction between microglia and neurons contributes to forgetting of remote memories (P70–P84).
source: The interaction between microglia and neurons has been demonstrated to contribute to synaptic modulation during motor learning (P30 and P60) (Parkhurst et al., 2013), sensory plasticity (P30) (Tremblay et al., 2010), forgetting of remote memories (P70–P84) (Wang et al., 2020), and chronic stress-related synaptic remodeling (P60-120) (Milior et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2020.

claim: The interaction between microglia and neurons contributes to chronic stress-related synaptic remodeling (P60-120).
source: The interaction between microglia and neurons has been demonstrated to contribute to synaptic modulation during motor learning (P30 and P60) (Parkhurst et al., 2013), sensory plasticity (P30) (Tremblay et al., 2010), forgetting of remote memories (P70–P84) (Wang et al., 2020), and chronic stress-related synaptic remodeling (P60-120) (Milior et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Milior et al., 2016.

claim: Direct observation of structural plasticity caused by resting microglial contact with synapses in the healthy adult brain has been hampered due to the infrequency of sporadic structural synaptic alterations at this stage.
source: However, the direct observation of structural plasticity caused by resting microglial contact with synapses in the healthy adult brain has been hampered due to the infrequency of sporadic structural synaptic alterations at this stage (Grutzendler et al., 2002; Holtmaat et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Grutzendler et al., 2002 and Holtmaat et al., 2006.

claim: The study used 16 adult (3–4 months old at the beginning of imaging) Cx3cr1Cre/Tomato x GFPM Thy-1 male mice.
source: We used two-photon microscopy to visualize the structural dynamics of microglia and their interactions with dendritic spines and axonal boutons in 16 adult (3–4 months old at the beginning of imaging) Cx3cr1Cre/Tomato x GFPM Thy-1 male mice, which expressed red fluorescent protein (tdTomato) in all microglia cells and enhanced green fluorescent protein (EGFP) in a subset of cortical pyramidal neurons (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental subjects used in the study.

claim: The transgenic mice expressed red fluorescent protein (tdTomato) in all microglia cells.
source: We used two-photon microscopy to visualize the structural dynamics of microglia and their interactions with dendritic spines and axonal boutons in 16 adult (3–4 months old at the beginning of imaging) Cx3cr1Cre/Tomato x GFPM Thy-1 male mice, which expressed red fluorescent protein (tdTomato) in all microglia cells and enhanced green fluorescent protein (EGFP) in a subset of cortical pyramidal neurons (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the fluorescent labeling system used in the study.

claim: The transgenic mice expressed enhanced green fluorescent protein (EGFP) in a subset of cortical pyramidal neurons.
source: We used two-photon microscopy to visualize the structural dynamics of microglia and their interactions with dendritic spines and axonal boutons in 16 adult (3–4 months old at the beginning of imaging) Cx3cr1Cre/Tomato x GFPM Thy-1 male mice, which expressed red fluorescent protein (tdTomato) in all microglia cells and enhanced green fluorescent protein (EGFP) in a subset of cortical pyramidal neurons (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the fluorescent labeling system used in the study.

claim: The retrosplenial cortex (RSC) was chosen for imaging as an area crucial for spatial navigation, memory, and history-dependent value coding.
source: The retrosplenial cortex (RSC) was chosen for imaging as an area crucial for spatial navigation, memory, and history-dependent value coding (Hattori et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hattori et al., 2019.

claim: The contact area between microglia and dendrites/axons increased after all types of photodamage in comparison with the baseline.
source: The contact area between microglia and dendrites/axons, defined by colocalization of microglia and neurons, increased after all types of photodamage in comparison with the baseline.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 1C2, D2, E2.

claim: The temporal profiles of fast-onset expansion in the contact area were similar in Spine-PD and Near-Spine-PD experiments and different from the slow increase in the contact area observed in the Near-Bouton-PD experiments.
source: The temporal profiles of fast-onset expansion in the contact area were similar in Spine-PD and Near-Spine-PD experiments and different from the slow increase in the contact area observed in the Near-Bouton-PD experiments (Figure 1C2,D2,E2, and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 1C2, D2, E2 and source data 1.

claim: The mean microglia-neuron contact area increased during 2 hr, from 0.53% before photodamage to 4.39% after Spine-PD.
source: The mean microglia-neuron contact area increased during 2 hr, from 0.53% and 0.24% before photodamage to 4.39% and 3.79% after Spine-PD and Near-Spine-PD, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data.

claim: The mean microglia-neuron contact area increased during 2 hr, from 0.24% before photodamage to 3.79% after Near-Spine-PD.
source: The mean microglia-neuron contact area increased during 2 hr, from 0.53% and 0.24% before photodamage to 4.39% and 3.79% after Spine-PD and Near-Spine-PD, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data.

claim: The microglia-neuron contact area was significantly higher in Spine-PD than in Near-Spine-PD and Near-Bouton-PD.
source: The microglia-neuron contact area was significantly higher in Spine-PD than in Near-Spine-PD and Near-Bouton-PD (Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is a finding supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 1—source data 2.

claim: The number of microglia-contacted synaptic sites increased after Spine-PD and Near-Spine-PD but not after Near-Bouton-PD, compared with the baseline.
source: More detailed analysis of contacts per spine and bouton revealed that the number of microglia-contacted synaptic sites increased after Spine-PD and Near-Spine-PD but not after Near-Bouton-PD, compared with the baseline (Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is a finding supported by detailed analysis shown in Figure 1—source data 2.

claim: The contact between microglial processes and spines/boutons lasted much longer after Spine-PD (60.97 ± 3.33 min) than during baseline imaging (~23.77 ± 4.9 min for spines).
source: Strikingly, the contact between microglial processes and spines/boutons lasted much longer after Spine-PD (60.97 ± 3.33 min), Near-Spine-PD (50.33 ± 3.22 min), or Near-Bouton-PD (70.57 ± 6.35 min) than during baseline imaging (~23.77 ± 4.9 min for spines and 21.18 ± 2.53 min for boutons) (Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 1—source data 2.

claim: The contact between microglial processes and spines/boutons lasted much longer after Near-Spine-PD (50.33 ± 3.22 min) than during baseline imaging (~23.77 ± 4.9 min for spines).
source: Strikingly, the contact between microglial processes and spines/boutons lasted much longer after Spine-PD (60.97 ± 3.33 min), Near-Spine-PD (50.33 ± 3.22 min), or Near-Bouton-PD (70.57 ± 6.35 min) than during baseline imaging (~23.77 ± 4.9 min for spines and 21.18 ± 2.53 min for boutons) (Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 1—source data 2.

claim: The contact between microglial processes and spines/boutons lasted much longer after Near-Bouton-PD (70.57 ± 6.35 min) than during baseline imaging (21.18 ± 2.53 min for boutons).
source: Strikingly, the contact between microglial processes and spines/boutons lasted much longer after Spine-PD (60.97 ± 3.33 min), Near-Spine-PD (50.33 ± 3.22 min), or Near-Bouton-PD (70.57 ± 6.35 min) than during baseline imaging (~23.77 ± 4.9 min for spines and 21.18 ± 2.53 min for boutons) (Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 1—source data 2.

claim: The prolonged duration of the contact between microglia processes and spines/boutons found after photodamage is similar to the values reported after induction of ischemia.
source: The prolonged duration of the contact between microglia processes and spines/boutons found after photodamage is similar to the values reported after induction of ischemia (Wake et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement compares the current findings to previously published data cited from Wake et al., 2009.

claim: All types of photodamage resulted in a higher turnover of spines and axonal boutons compared with the baseline.
source: All types of photodamage resulted in a higher turnover of spines and axonal boutons compared with the baseline (Figure 1—source data 1 and Figure 1—Videos 1–3), when spine and bouton turnover rates were less than 0.05%.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 1—source data 1 and Figure 1—Videos 1–3.

claim: Spine and bouton turnover rates were less than 0.05% during baseline imaging.
source: All types of photodamage resulted in a higher turnover of spines and axonal boutons compared with the baseline (Figure 1—source data 1 and Figure 1—Videos 1–3), when spine and bouton turnover rates were less than 0.05%.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the baseline experimental data.

claim: The temporal dynamics of turnover matched those of microglia-neuron contact during the 2 hr evaluation period.
source: Importantly, the temporal dynamics of turnover matched those of microglia-neuron contact during the 2 hr evaluation period (Figure 1C2,D2,E2, and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 1C2, D2, E2 and Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: Mean turnover over the 2 hr of observation was higher after Spine-PD compared with other photodamage types.
source: To summarize the remodeling of spines and boutons, we calculated a mean turnover over the 2 hr of observation. It was higher after Spine-PD compared with other photodamage types (Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 1—source data 2.

claim: There were no differences between the percentages of gained and lost spines after Spine-PD and Near-Spine-PD.
source: There were no differences between the percentages of gained and lost spines after Spine-PD and Near-Spine-PD (Figure 1C3,D3).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 1C3 and D3.

claim: The rate of bouton formation after Near-Bouton-PD was higher than the elimination rate.
source: However, the rate of bouton formation after Near-Bouton-PD was higher than the elimination rate (Figure 1E3).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 1E3.

claim: Spine-head filopodia and new filopodia at boutons were observed after Spine-PD/Near-Spine-PD and Near-Bouton-PD, respectively.
source: Interestingly, we observed the formation of spine-head filopodia and new filopodia at boutons after Spine-PD/Near-Spine-PD and Near-Bouton-PD, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2 and Figure 1—Videos 4–6).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2 and Figure 1—Videos 4–6.

claim: Spine-head filopodia and new filopodia at boutons were not observed during the baseline period.
source: These structures were not observed during the baseline period and have been suggested to be important for the formation of multiple spine synapses following induction of long-term potentiation (Toni et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a finding from the baseline experimental data.

claim: Spine-head filopodia have been suggested to be important for the formation of multiple spine synapses following induction of long-term potentiation.
source: These structures were not observed during the baseline period and have been suggested to be important for the formation of multiple spine synapses following induction of long-term potentiation (Toni et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Toni et al., 1999.

claim: The filopodia occurrence rate after Near-Bouton-PD (79.55%) was remarkably higher than after Spine-PD (11.98%) and Near-Spine-PD (23.61%).
source: The filopodia occurrence rate after Near-Bouton-PD (79.55%) was remarkably higher than after Spine-PD (11.98%) and Near-Spine-PD (23.61%) (Figure 1C4,D4,E4).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by data shown in Figure 1C4, D4, E4.

claim: All the boutons which formed filopodia were apparently contacted by microglia for an average duration of 87 ± 33.7 min.
source: All the boutons which formed filopodia were apparently contacted by microglia for an average duration of 87 ± 33.7 min.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data.

claim: New and transient spines and boutons were closest to the photodamage site.
source: New and transient spines and boutons were closest to the photodamage site (Figure 2A2,B2,C2 and Figure 2A3,B3,C3) and were more often in contact with microglia when compared with stable spines/boutons after all types of photodamage (Figure 2A4,B4,C4).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 2A2, B2, C2, A3, B3, C3.

claim: New and transient spines and boutons were more often in contact with microglia when compared with stable spines/boutons after all types of photodamage.
source: New and transient spines and boutons were closest to the photodamage site (Figure 2A2,B2,C2 and Figure 2A3,B3,C3) and were more often in contact with microglia when compared with stable spines/boutons after all types of photodamage (Figure 2A4,B4,C4).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 2A4, B4, C4.

claim: The duration of the microglial contact was longer with the newly formed and lost spines than with the stable spines.
source: The duration of the microglial contact was longer with the newly formed and lost spines than with the stable spines (Figure 2A5,B5,C5).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 2A5, B5, C5.

claim: After Near-Spine-PD the filopodia always appeared at stable spines.
source: After Near-Spine-PD the filopodia always appeared at stable spines, while after Near-Bouton-PD the filopodia originated more often at newly formed than at stable or lost boutons (Figure 2A6,B6,C6).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 2A6, B6, C6.

claim: After Near-Bouton-PD the filopodia originated more often at newly formed than at stable or lost boutons.
source: After Near-Spine-PD the filopodia always appeared at stable spines, while after Near-Bouton-PD the filopodia originated more often at newly formed than at stable or lost boutons (Figure 2A6,B6,C6).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 2A6, B6, C6.

claim: PLX3397 is an inhibitor of colony-stimulating factor one receptor, the activity of which is vitally important to microglial cells.
source: To test this hypothesis, we depleted microglia in the whole brain using PLX3397 as an inhibitor of colony-stimulating factor one receptor, the activity of which is vitally important to microglial cells (Elmore et al., 2014; Spiller et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Elmore et al., 2014 and Spiller et al., 2018.

claim: The number of microglia was dramatically reduced after 1 week of PLX3397 treatment and dropped to 0.6% after 4 weeks.
source: The number of microglia was dramatically reduced after 1 week of PLX3397 treatment and dropped to 0.6% after 4 weeks (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: PLX3397 treatment did not affect the turnover of spines/boutons during baseline imaging.
source: During baseline imaging, we observed that PLX3397 treatment did not affect the turnover of spines/boutons, which remained very low before and after the treatment in both the control and treated groups (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B,F,J).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B, F, J.

claim: The depletion of microglia resulted in suppression of the spine turnover associated with photodamage.
source: However, the depletion of microglia resulted in suppression of the spine turnover associated with photodamage.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the microglia depletion experiments.

claim: Turnover in the PLX3397-treated group decreased after Spine-PD (19.13 ± 3.35 vs. 4.51 ± 3.97, p<0.001).
source: Comparing mean turnover values before and after PLX3397/control-treatment for each type of photodamage, we detected no differences in the control group (Figure 3C2,D2,E2), while turnover in the PLX3397-treated group decreased only after Spine-PD (19.13 ± 3.35 vs. 4.51 ± 3.97, p<0.001, Tukey's post-hoc test) and Near-Spine-PD (6.38 ± 2.40 vs. 0.93 ± 1.06, p<0.001, Tukey's post-hoc test) and not after Near-Bouton-PD (Figure 3C2,D2,E2, Figure 3—source datas 1 and 2 and Figure 3—Videos 1–3).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by statistical analysis and data shown in Figure 3C2, D2, E2.

claim: Turnover in the PLX3397-treated group decreased after Near-Spine-PD (6.38 ± 2.40 vs. 0.93 ± 1.06, p<0.001).
source: Comparing mean turnover values before and after PLX3397/control-treatment for each type of photodamage, we detected no differences in the control group (Figure 3C2,D2,E2), while turnover in the PLX3397-treated group decreased only after Spine-PD (19.13 ± 3.35 vs. 4.51 ± 3.97, p<0.001, Tukey's post-hoc test) and Near-Spine-PD (6.38 ± 2.40 vs. 0.93 ± 1.06, p<0.001, Tukey's post-hoc test) and not after Near-Bouton-PD (Figure 3C2,D2,E2, Figure 3—source datas 1 and 2 and Figure 3—Videos 1–3).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by statistical analysis and data shown in Figure 3C2, D2, E2.

claim: Turnover in the PLX3397-treated group did not decrease after Near-Bouton-PD.
source: Comparing mean turnover values before and after PLX3397/control-treatment for each type of photodamage, we detected no differences in the control group (Figure 3C2,D2,E2), while turnover in the PLX3397-treated group decreased only after Spine-PD (19.13 ± 3.35 vs. 4.51 ± 3.97, p<0.001, Tukey's post-hoc test) and Near-Spine-PD (6.38 ± 2.40 vs. 0.93 ± 1.06, p<0.001, Tukey's post-hoc test) and not after Near-Bouton-PD (Figure 3C2,D2,E2, Figure 3—source datas 1 and 2 and Figure 3—Videos 1–3).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 3C2, D2, E2.

claim: Depletion of microglia reduced the mean percentages of gained and lost spines after Spine-PD and Near-Spine-PD.
source: Detailed analysis of the turnover revealed that depletion of microglia reduced the mean percentages of gained and lost spines after Spine-PD and Near-Spine-PD (Figure 3C3,D3,E3) and of bouton filopodia induced by Near-Bouton-PD (Figure 3C4,D4,E4).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 3C3, D3, E3.

claim: Depletion of microglia reduced bouton filopodia induced by Near-Bouton-PD.
source: Detailed analysis of the turnover revealed that depletion of microglia reduced the mean percentages of gained and lost spines after Spine-PD and Near-Spine-PD (Figure 3C3,D3,E3) and of bouton filopodia induced by Near-Bouton-PD (Figure 3C4,D4,E4).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 3C4, D4, E4.

claim: There was no effect of PLX3397 on filopodia length.
source: There was, however, no effect of PLX3397 on filopodia length (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C,G,K) or stability (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D,H,L).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C, G, K.

claim: There was no effect of PLX3397 on filopodia stability.
source: There was, however, no effect of PLX3397 on filopodia length (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C,G,K) or stability (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D,H,L).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D, H, L.

claim: Spine-head filopodia formation was independent of microglia.
source: Also, spine-head filopodia formation was independent of microglia (Figure 3C4,D4).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 3C4, D4.

claim: Microglia react rapidly to photodamaged synapses in the mature brain and establish prominent contacts with synaptic structures to promote spine turnover.
source: These observations provide evidence that microglia react rapidly to photodamaged synapses in the mature brain and establish prominent contacts with synaptic structures to promote spine turnover, in agreement with studies of sporadic synaptic remodeling in the neocortex and somatosensory cortex of adult mice (Akiyoshi et al., 2018; Parkhurst et al., 2013; Wake et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and supported by citations to Akiyoshi et al., 2018; Parkhurst et al., 2013; Wake et al., 2009.

claim: The approach with targeting of single synaptic sites makes an important advance to minimize the injury and standardize the signal that acutely drives microglial approach and interaction with neurons, as compared to previous studies using single-cell or single-neurite laser-mediated photoablation.
source: We think that our approach with targeting of single synaptic sites makes an important advance to minimize the injury and standardize the signal that acutely drives microglial approach and interaction with neurons, as compared to previous studies using single-cell or single-neurite laser-mediated photoablation (Canty et al., 2013; Go et al., 2016; Haynes et al., 2006; Stoyanov et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the methodological contribution of the study, supported by citations to Canty et al., 2013; Go et al., 2016; Haynes et al., 2006; Stoyanov et al., 2020.

claim: An important component of the signal that attracts microglia is photodamage-released adenosine triphosphate (ATP) that attracts microglia via activation of P2Y12 receptors.
source: An important component of that signal, as shown in single-cell photoablation studies, is photodamage-released adenosine triphosphate (ATP) that attracts microglia via activation of P2Y12 receptors (Haynes et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Haynes et al., 2006.

claim: The observed microglia-mediated increase in the rates of spine and bouton filopodia formation might provide a substrate for formation of new associations.
source: The observed microglia-mediated increase in the rates of spine and bouton filopodia formation might provide a substrate for formation of new associations and may be mediated by BDNF released by microglia (Parkhurst et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings, indicated by the word 'might'.

claim: The observed microglia-mediated increase in the rates of spine and bouton filopodia formation may be mediated by BDNF released by microglia.
source: The observed microglia-mediated increase in the rates of spine and bouton filopodia formation might provide a substrate for formation of new associations and may be mediated by BDNF released by microglia (Parkhurst et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings, indicated by the word 'may', and supported by a citation to Parkhurst et al., 2013.

claim: BDNF release from microglia and TrkB phosphorylation in neurons can be strongly stimulated by the binding of ATP to the purinergic receptor P2X4R.
